questions.question: Which of these isomers has the highest boiling temperature? (The isomer structures are in a diagram shown in the figure below.)
steps: The four structures are isomers, each with one polar C-Cl bond, so they have the same number of electrons and similar dipoles.
Boiling temperature depends on how strong the intermolecular forces (mainly London forces) are between the molecules.
A has no side chains, so its long molecules lie side by side with the largest surface area of contact and the most London forces.
Branching (B, then C, then D which is the most branched) makes the molecule more compact, so there is less contact and weaker London forces.
More energy is needed to separate the molecules of A, so A has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which property is NOT due to hydrogen bonding? A: ice is less dense than water at 0 deg C; B: HF has a higher boiling temperature than HCl; C: H-H bond enthalpy is greater than Si-H bond enthalpy; D: alcohols are less volatile than alkanes of similar molar mass.
questions.answer: C (H-H bond enthalpy is greater than Si-H bond enthalpy)
steps: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force that affects density, boiling temperature and volatility.
A: ice has an open hydrogen-bonded lattice, so it is less dense than water - due to hydrogen bonding.
B: HF molecules hydrogen bond to each other, so HF boils higher than HCl - due to hydrogen bonding.
D: alcohols hydrogen bond between molecules, so they are less volatile than alkanes - due to hydrogen bonding.
C: bond enthalpy is the energy of a covalent bond within a molecule, not an intermolecular force.
So the answer is C.

questions.question: Which diagram best represents a hydrogen bond between two water molecules? (The diagrams A-D are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: A: dotted line from the H of one water molecule to the O of the other, in a straight line (180 deg) with the O-H bond
steps: A hydrogen bond forms between a delta+ H (bonded to O) on one molecule and a lone pair on the delta- O of a neighbouring molecule.
It is drawn as a dotted line from H to O, lying in a straight line with the covalent O-H bond, so the O-H...O angle is 180 deg: this is A.
B is wrong: the dotted line joins H to H, and two delta+ hydrogens attract nothing.
C is wrong: it marks 104.5 deg at the hydrogen bond, but 104.5 deg is the H-O-H bond angle inside a molecule, not the O-H...O angle.
D is wrong: the O-H...O arrangement is bent, and 104.5 deg is again the angle within one molecule.

questions.question: What are the strongest interactions between molecules in solid hydrogen iodide, HI? A: covalent bonds; B: hydrogen bonds; C: ionic bonds; D: London forces.
steps: Covalent bonds (A) join atoms within one HI molecule, not between molecules.
Ionic bonds (C) do not occur in HI, which is a covalent molecule.
Hydrogen bonds (B) need H bonded to F, O or N; the H in HI is not bonded to such an atom.
Between HI molecules the intermolecular forces are London forces and permanent dipole forces.
Of the options given, London forces (D) is the only intermolecular interaction listed.
So the answer is D.

questions.question: Three isomers X, Y and Z are shown as skeletal formulae. Which series gives the correct order of increasing boiling temperature? (A: Y, X, Z; B: X, Y, Z; C: Y, Z, X; D: X, Z, Y.)
steps: Read the skeletal formulae: Y is hexane (straight chain), Z is 3-methylpentane, X is 2,2-dimethylbutane. All are C6H14 and non-polar, so only London forces act.
More branching makes a molecule more compact, so there is less surface area of contact between molecules and weaker London forces.
Y is unbranched, so it has the strongest London forces and the highest boiling temperature.
X is the most branched, so it has the weakest London forces and the lowest boiling temperature; Z lies between.
Increasing boiling temperature: X < Z < Y, which is option D.

questions.question: Which statement about water is NOT due to hydrogen bonding? A: water has a less open structure than ice; B: ice cubes float; C: volume increases when water freezes; D: water is a good solvent for ionic compounds.
questions.answer: D (water is a good solvent for ionic compounds)
steps: A: the open lattice of ice comes from hydrogen bonds, so the water-ice contrast is due to hydrogen bonding.
B: ice floats because its open hydrogen-bonded lattice makes it less dense than water.
C: the open lattice of ice gives a larger volume on freezing, which is due to hydrogen bonding.
D: water dissolves ionic compounds by ion-dipole attractions between ions and polar water molecules.
So D is the statement not due to hydrogen bonding.

questions.question: Add arrowheads and stoichiometric coefficients to the Hess's Law diagram for the combustion of propane and the formation of propane.
questions.answer: Arrows: elements to C3H8 (formation); C3H8 + 5O2 to 3CO2 + 4H2O (combustion); elements to products via 3C + 3O2 and 4H2 + 2O2 (5 O2 in total).
steps: Enthalpy of formation: 3C(s) + 4H2(g) -> C3H8(g), arrow from the elements up to propane.
Enthalpy of combustion: C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) -> 3CO2(g) + 4H2O, arrow from propane to the products.
Direct route from elements to products: 3C(s) + 3O2(g) -> 3CO2(g) and 4H2(g) + 2O2(g) -> 4H2O.
The O2 coefficients add to 5 (3 + 2), matching the combustion equation.
Arrowheads point from the reactant side to the product side of each step.

questions.question: Use the enthalpy data at the start of Q6 and the Hess's Law diagram to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propane, with sign and units.
steps: The diagram gives two routes from the elements to 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(l): direct (formation of the products) and via propane (formation of propane then its combustion).
So Delta fH(C3H8) + Delta cH(C3H8) = 3 x Delta fH(CO2) + 4 x Delta fH(H2O), which gives Delta fH(C3H8) = [3 x Delta fH(CO2) + 4 x Delta fH(H2O)] - Delta cH(C3H8).
3 x (-393.5) = -1180.5 and 4 x (-285.8) = -1143.2, so the direct route totals -2323.7 kJ mol^-1.
Delta fH(C3H8) = -2323.7 - (-2219) = -104.7 kJ mol^-1 (negative: formation of propane is exothermic).

questions.question: Explain why the successive increases in the values for the straight-chain alkanes (boiling temperatures and standard enthalpies of combustion) are similar.
questions.answer: Each extra CH2 group adds the same bonds and London forces, so each step gives a similar rise in boiling temperature and in enthalpy of combustion.
steps: Successive straight-chain alkanes differ by one CH2 group.
Each CH2 group adds one C-C bond and two C-H bonds to the molecule.
The same bonds are added each time, so the enthalpy of combustion rises by a similar amount per step.
Each CH2 group adds the same number of electrons and surface area, so London forces rise by a similar amount each step.
More energy is needed to separate molecules with stronger London forces, so boiling temperatures rise by a similar amount each step.

questions.question: The increase in one of the tabulated values from butane to pentane is smaller than any other increase. Suggest an explanation.
questions.answer: At 298 K butane is a gas but pentane is a liquid, so some energy is needed to vaporise pentane before it burns, and less energy is released
steps: Standard enthalpies of combustion refer to the fuel in its standard state at 298 K. The table gives boiling temperatures of -0.5 deg C for butane and 36.1 deg C for pentane.
So butane is a gas, while pentane (like hexane and heptane) is a liquid at 298 K.
Burning liquid pentane involves first overcoming its London forces to vaporise it, which takes in energy, so less net energy is released (a less exothermic value).
The other increases compare two gases (C2 to C4) or two liquids (C5 to C7), so only the butane to pentane step (632 against about 655) is smaller.

questions.question: Explain, with reference to intermolecular forces (no detailed description needed), why the boiling temperatures of alkanes increase as the number of carbon atoms increases.
questions.answer: More carbon atoms give more electrons and a larger molecule, so London forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
steps: Alkane molecules are non-polar, so the only intermolecular forces between them are London forces.
Larger alkanes have more electrons, so their electron clouds are more polarisable.
More polarisable molecules form larger instantaneous and induced dipoles, so London forces are stronger.
Longer chains have a larger surface area of contact between neighbouring molecules, giving more London force interactions.
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger London forces and separate the molecules.
So boiling temperature increases with the number of carbon atoms.

questions.question: Four liquid organic compounds are compared by timing an air bubble in inverted tubes. For which compound does the bubble take the longest time?
steps: The bubble rises slowest through the most viscous liquid, so the longest time means the highest viscosity.
Viscosity is higher when the intermolecular forces are stronger, because the molecules cannot slide past each other as easily.
Each OH group can form hydrogen bonds. A has one OH, B has two and C has three, so C forms the most extensive hydrogen-bonded network.
D has no O-H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself (only London and permanent dipole forces), so it is less viscous than C.
So C has the greatest viscosity and the longest bubble time.

questions.question: Which pure compound has hydrogen bonding in the liquid state? A: 1,1,1-trichloroethane, CH3CCl3; B: trimethylamine, (CH3)3N; C: hydrogen fluoride, HF; D: hydrogen sulfide, H2S.
steps: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to a small, highly electronegative atom: F, O or N.
A: in CH3CCl3 the H is bonded only to C, so there is no hydrogen bonding.
B: in (CH3)3N the N has no H bonded to it, so there is no hydrogen bonding.
C: in HF the H is bonded to F, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules.
D: in H2S the H is bonded to S, which is not electronegative enough, so there is no hydrogen bonding.
So the answer is C.

questions.question: Which of these isomers has the highest boiling temperature? (The isomer structures are in a diagram shown in the figure below.)
steps: The four structures are isomers of the same alkane, so each has the same number of electrons and only London forces.
A is the straight chain; B (2-methylpentane), C (3-methylpentane) and D (2,3-dimethylbutane) have side chains.
The unbranched molecule has the largest surface area of contact, so the strongest London forces.
More energy is needed to separate the molecules of A, so A has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which row shows the hydrogen halides in order of increasing boiling temperature? (The rows are in a table shown in the figure below.)
steps: Boiling temperatures: HCl -85.0 deg C, HBr about -67 deg C, HI -35.1 deg C, HF +19.5 deg C.
From HCl to HI the molecules have more electrons, so London forces strengthen and the boiling temperature rises.
HF is out of line and highest because its molecules form hydrogen bonds (H bonded to the very electronegative, small F).
So increasing boiling temperature is HCl < HBr < HI < HF, which is row C.

questions.question: Which isomer of C8H18 has the lowest boiling temperature? A: 2,5-dimethylhexane; B: 2-methylheptane; C: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane; D: octane.
steps: All four are C8H18 isomers, so they have the same molar mass and only London forces between molecules.
Branching makes molecules more compact and reduces their surface area of contact.
Less contact means weaker London forces between molecules.
Weaker London forces need less energy to overcome, so the boiling temperature is lower.
C is the most branched isomer, so it has the lowest boiling temperature; D (octane) is the straight chain with the highest.

questions.question: Which compound has the highest boiling temperature? (The options are in a diagram shown in the figure below.)
steps: The options are A propan-2-ol, B propan-1-ol, C butane and D 2-methylpropane.
The alcohols (A, B) form hydrogen bonds between molecules as well as London forces, so they boil far higher than the alkanes C and D, which have only London forces.
Of the two alcohols, propan-1-ol is straight-chain, so its molecules have a larger surface area of contact and stronger London forces than the branched propan-2-ol.
So propan-1-ol (B) has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which solvent dissolves the greatest amount of the hydrocarbon C35H72? A: butan-1-ol; B: ethanoic acid; C: hexane; D: water.
steps: C35H72 is a large non-polar alkane, so its molecules have only London forces between them.
Like dissolves like: non-polar solutes dissolve best in non-polar solvents.
Hexane is non-polar and has London forces, so it mixes readily with the alkane.
Butan-1-ol, ethanoic acid and water are polar and hydrogen bond to each other, so they do not mix well with the alkane.
So hexane (C) dissolves the greatest amount.

questions.question: Which statement about ice is NOT correct? A: ice has a lower density than water; B: H2O molecules are further apart in ice than in water; C: the H-O-H bond angle is the same in ice and water; D: H2O molecules in ice are held together by hydrogen bonds.
questions.answer: C (the H-O-H bond angle is not the same in ice and water)
steps: A: hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice, so ice is less dense than water - correct.
B: the open lattice keeps the molecules further apart in ice than in liquid water - correct.
D: hydrogen bonds hold H2O molecules together in ice - correct.
C: the H-O-H angle is about 104.5 deg in liquid water, but it differs in the ice lattice, so the statement is incorrect.
So the answer is C.

questions.question: Which intermolecular forces exist between the molecules of the compound shown? (The compound structure is in a diagram shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: D: hydrogen bonding, permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces and London forces
steps: The compound is HOCH2CH2CHO: it has an O-H group and a C=O group.
The O-H group (H bonded to O, with a lone pair on O in neighbouring molecules) allows hydrogen bonding between molecules.
The polar C=O group gives permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.
All molecules have London forces, so all three types are present: D.

questions.question: Which compound does NOT form hydrogen bonds between its molecules? A: HCl; B: H2O; C: HF; D: NH3.
steps: Hydrogen bonds need H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom: F, O or N.
B (H2O), C (HF) and D (NH3) all have H bonded to O, F or N, so they form hydrogen bonds.
A: in HCl the H is bonded to Cl, which is not electronegative enough to form hydrogen bonds.
HCl molecules are held together only by dipole-dipole and London forces.
So the answer is A.

questions.question: Why is the boiling temperature of hydrogen iodide higher than that of hydrogen bromide? A: HI has stronger London forces than HBr; B: HI has a larger permanent dipole than HBr; C: HI has stronger hydrogen bonds than HBr; D: the H-I bond is stronger than the H-Br bond.
questions.answer: A (HI has stronger London forces than HBr)
steps: HI and HBr are simple covalent molecules with no hydrogen bonding.
HI has more electrons and a larger electron cloud than HBr, so it is more polarisable.
A larger electron cloud gives stronger London forces between molecules.
More energy is needed to separate HI molecules, so HI boils at a higher temperature.
B is wrong because HI is less polar than HBr; D is wrong because bond strength is not overcome on boiling.

questions.question: Which compound would be expected to have the highest boiling temperature? A: (CH3)3COH; B: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH; C: CH3CH2CH(CH3)2; D: CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3.
steps: A and B are alcohols, so they form hydrogen bonds; C and D are alkanes with only London forces.
A is highly branched (tertiary), so its molecules pack less closely and have less surface contact.
B is a straight-chain alcohol, giving a larger surface area of contact and stronger London forces as well as hydrogen bonds.
C and D have only London forces, so they boil at lower temperatures.
So B (butan-1-ol) has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which of these alkanes (A: butane; B: hexane; C: pentane; D: propane) has the highest boiling temperature?
steps: All four are straight-chain alkanes with only London forces between molecules.
Boiling temperature rises with chain length because more electrons give stronger London forces.
Hexane has the most carbon atoms of the four (C6).
So hexane (B) has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which of these alkanes (skeletal formulae A to D, all isomers of C7H16) has the lowest boiling temperature?
steps: The four structures are isomers of C7H16: A is 2,4-dimethylpentane, B is 3-methylhexane, C is 2-methylhexane and D is heptane.
All are non-polar, so only London forces act, and each has the same number of electrons.
More branching gives a more compact molecule with a smaller surface area of contact, so weaker London forces.
A has the most branching, so it has the weakest London forces and the lowest boiling temperature (D, unbranched, is the highest).

questions.question: Which row in the table shows the forces between the molecules in the liquid state? (The table is shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: D: H2S (London forces and permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions, no hydrogen bonding)
steps: H2S is a bent, polar molecule, so it has permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces as well as London forces.
S is not electronegative enough for hydrogen bonding, so the row ticks London forces and permanent dipole forces and crosses hydrogen bonding: D.
A is wrong: BF3 is symmetrical and non-polar, but every molecule has London forces, so the row should not show London forces crossed.
B is wrong: CH4 is non-polar and cannot hydrogen bond (C-H is not polar enough).
C is wrong: NH3 does form hydrogen bonds (N-H and a lone pair on N), but the row shows none.

questions.question: Use mean bond enthalpies to calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of octane, C8H18. (The balanced equation and the bond enthalpy values are shown in the figure below.)
steps: Equation: C8H18 + 12.5 O2 -> 8CO2 + 9H2O. Bonds broken: 7 C-C, 18 C-H and 12.5 O=O.
Bonds formed: 16 C=O (in 8CO2) and 18 O-H (in 9H2O).
Energy released forming bonds = (16 x 805) + (18 x 464) = 12880 + 8352 = 21232 kJ.
Enthalpy change = bonds broken - bonds formed = 16088 - 21232 = -5144 kJ mol^-1.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the standard enthalpy change of combustion of octane (-5470 kJ mol-1) differs from the value calculated using bond enthalpy data.
questions.answer: (1) Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds; (2) the standard value uses standard conditions and products in their standard states (e.g. liquid water), unlike the gas-phase bond data.
steps: Mean bond enthalpies are averages taken from many different compounds, so they are approximate for octane.
Bond enthalpies refer to gaseous species, whereas the standard value uses substances in their standard states.
Standard conditions (298 K and 100 kPa) are fixed, which bond enthalpy calculations do not specify.
In the standard value water is liquid, so more energy is released than if steam were formed.

questions.question: 1 kg of petrol is assumed to be pure octane, with standard enthalpy change of combustion -5470 kJ mol-1. The energy used to move the car is 11 MJ. Calculate the percentage of the maximum energy that is available to move the car.
steps: Molar mass of octane, C8H18 = (8 x 12.0) + (18 x 1.0) = 114 g mol-1.
Moles of octane in 1000 g = 1000 / 114 = 8.77 mol.
Maximum energy from 1 kg = 8.77 x 5470 kJ = approx. 48 000 kJ = 48.0 MJ.
Percentage available = (11 / 48.0) x 100 = 22.9%, which is about 23%.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the energy used to move the car is less than the theoretical maximum energy from the fuel.
questions.answer: Heat is lost to the surroundings (engine and exhaust), and energy is used to overcome friction and air resistance (or combustion is incomplete).
steps: Not all the fuel burns completely, so some of its chemical energy is not released as heat.
Heat energy is lost to the surroundings through the engine block and the hot exhaust gases.
Some energy is used to overcome friction between moving parts of the engine.
Energy used to overcome air resistance and friction does not move the car forward, so less energy is available for motion.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the intermolecular forces involved when hydrogen and ammonia liquefy, describing how these forces are formed.
questions.answer: Hydrogen has only London forces from temporary dipoles; ammonia has hydrogen bonds (N-H...N) and dipole-dipole forces as well as London forces, so ammonia liquefies more easily.
steps: Hydrogen is a non-polar molecule, so its only intermolecular forces are London forces.
London forces form when electron movement creates a temporary dipole that induces dipoles in neighbouring molecules.
These forces are weak because H2 has only two electrons, so hydrogen must be cooled to very low temperatures to liquefy.
Ammonia is polar (N-H bonds and a lone pair on N), so it has permanent dipole-dipole forces between molecules.
Ammonia also forms hydrogen bonds: the lone pair on N attracts the delta+ H of a neighbouring N-H group.
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than London forces, so ammonia liquefies more easily than hydrogen.
Contrast: both are intermolecular, but H2 has only London forces while NH3 also has hydrogen bonds and dipole-dipole forces.

questions.question: Hexane boils at 69 deg C and cyclohexane at 81 deg C. The main reason cyclohexane has the higher boiling temperature is that its molecules A: have more electrons; B: have strong permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces; C: have a larger surface area of contact; D: form hydrogen bonds.
questions.answer: C (have a larger surface area of contact)
steps: Both are non-polar hydrocarbons, so the intermolecular forces between them are London forces only.
A is wrong: cyclohexane (C6H12) has fewer electrons than hexane (C6H14).
B and D are wrong: neither molecule is polar enough for dipole-dipole forces, and neither has H bonded to F, O or N.
The rigid ring of cyclohexane lets molecules pack more closely, increasing the surface area of contact.
Greater contact gives stronger London forces, so more energy is needed to boil cyclohexane.
So the answer is C.

questions.question: Which structure best represents a hydrogen bond between methanol and water? (The structures are in a diagram shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: A: dotted line from the O lone pair of methanol to the H of the water O-H, in a straight line O...H-O
steps: A hydrogen bond links a lone pair on an O atom (delta-) to a delta+ H that is bonded to O (or N or F).
In A, the dotted line joins the lone pair on the methanol O to the H of water, lying in a straight line with the O-H bond (O...H-O about 180 deg).
B has the same atoms linked, but the water O-H is drawn bent away from the hydrogen bond, so it does not show the linear arrangement.
In C and D the dotted line goes to an H on the carbon (C-H), but C-H is almost non-polar so it cannot form a hydrogen bond.
So A is best.

questions.question: Which compound has intermolecular hydrogen bonding? A: (CH3)3N; B: (CH3)3CF; C: (CH3)3COH; D: (CH3)3CCHO.
steps: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to O, N or F.
A: N in (CH3)3N has no H bonded to it, so there is no hydrogen bonding.
B: the F is bonded only to C, so there is no H-F or hydrogen bonding.
C: (CH3)3COH has an O-H group, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules.
D: the C=O group has no O-H or N-H, so there is no hydrogen bonding.
So the answer is C.

questions.question: Which compound has London forces as its only intermolecular force? A: HF; B: OF2; C: PF3; D: CF4.
steps: A: HF forms hydrogen bonds.
B and C: OF2 and PF3 are polar molecules with permanent dipoles, so they have dipole-dipole forces.
D: CF4 is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so its polar C-F bonds cancel out and the molecule is non-polar.
Non-polar molecules have only London forces between them.
So the answer is D (CF4).

questions.question: Which of these compounds would be expected to have the highest boiling temperature? A: butan-1-ol; B: 2-methylpropan-1-ol; C: 2-methylpropan-2-ol; D: pentane.
steps: A, B and C are alcohols, so each forms hydrogen bonds; D is an alkane with London forces only.
C is highly branched (tertiary), so its molecules pack less closely and have less surface contact.
B is branched, so it has less surface contact than the straight-chain alcohol A.
A is a straight-chain alcohol, giving the largest surface area of contact and the strongest London forces alongside hydrogen bonds.
So A (butan-1-ol) has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the hydrogen halides in order of decreasing boiling temperature? (The sequences are shown in the figure below.)
steps: Boiling temperatures: HF 19.5 deg C, HI -35.1 deg C, HBr about -67 deg C, HCl -85 deg C.
HF is highest because its molecules form hydrogen bonds, the strongest of these intermolecular forces.
For the others, London forces strengthen with the number of electrons, so HI > HBr > HCl.
So the decreasing order is HF > HI > HBr > HCl: B.

questions.question: Propanal boils at a higher temperature than butane. The main reason is that propanal molecules A: have more electrons; B: have strong permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces; C: have a larger surface area of contact; D: form hydrogen bonds.
steps: Propanal (CH3CH2CHO) has a polar C=O group, so its molecules are polar.
Polar molecules have permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces between them, in addition to London forces.
Butane is non-polar, so its molecules have only London forces.
Propanal has no O-H or N-H bond, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds (D is wrong).
Butane has as many or more electrons than propanal, so A is wrong and the surface contact is similar (C is wrong).
So the answer is B.

questions.question: Which is the order of increasing boiling temperature for compounds W, X, Y and Z? (A: YZXW; B: YXZW; C: WXZY; D: XWYZ.) The compounds are shown in a diagram shown in the figure below.
steps: Read the structures: Y is butane, X is butan-1-ol (one OH), Z is butane-1,2-diol (two OH) and W is butane-1,2,3-triol (three OH).
Y has no O-H group, so only London forces act: it has the lowest boiling temperature.
X, Z and W form hydrogen bonds, and the number of hydrogen bonds per molecule rises with the number of OH groups (1, 2, 3).
More hydrogen bonding means more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so boiling temperature increases Y < X < Z < W (option B).

questions.question: Which alkane has the highest boiling temperature? A: 2,2-dimethylpropane; B: 2-methylbutane; C: butane; D: pentane.
steps: All four are alkanes, so only London forces act between their molecules.
Pentane is the straight-chain alkane with 5 carbons, giving it a large surface area of contact.
2,2-dimethylpropane and 2-methylbutane are branched, so they have less surface contact.
Butane is shorter than pentane, so it has fewer electrons and weaker London forces.
So D (pentane) has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which alkane has the strongest London forces in the liquid phase? A: (CH3)4C; B: CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3; C: (C2H5)4C; D: CH3(CH2)7CH3.
steps: London forces get stronger as molecules have more electrons and a larger surface area of contact.
A and B are small molecules (5 carbons), so their London forces are weak.
C, (C2H5)4C, has 9 carbons but is highly branched, so its molecules have little surface contact.
D, CH3(CH2)7CH3, is straight-chain nonane with 9 carbons and the largest surface area of contact.
So D has the strongest London forces.

questions.question: Which isomer has the highest boiling temperature? (The isomer options are in a diagram shown in the figure below.)
steps: The four structures are isomers of the same alkane, so each has only London forces and the same number of electrons.
A is the straight chain, B and C have one side chain each, and D has two methyl groups on one carbon, so D is the most branched.
The unbranched molecule has the largest surface area of contact, giving the strongest London forces.
So A has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which compound has the highest boiling temperature? A: pentane; B: cyclopentane; C: butan-1-ol; D: butane-1,4-diol.
steps: Pentane and cyclopentane have only London forces between their molecules.
Butan-1-ol has one -OH group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds.
Butane-1,4-diol has two -OH groups, so each molecule can form more hydrogen bonds.
More hydrogen bonds need more energy to separate the molecules, so it boils at the highest temperature.
So the answer is D.

questions.question: Which alkane has the highest boiling temperature? A: hexane; B: pentane; C: 2-methylpentane; D: 2,3-dimethylbutane.
steps: All four are alkanes with only London forces between molecules.
Hexane is the straight-chain alkane with the most carbon atoms of the four.
Its straight chain packs closely, giving the largest surface area of contact and the strongest London forces.
C and D are branched isomers with less surface contact, so their London forces are weaker.
So A (hexane) has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which compound has intermolecular hydrogen bonding? A: HF; B: H2Te; C: AsH3; D: SnH4.
steps: Hydrogen bonds need H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom: F, O or N.
A: HF has H bonded to F, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules.
B, C and D have H bonded to Te, As or Sn, which are not electronegative enough for hydrogen bonding.
These compounds are held together only by dipole-dipole and London forces.
So the answer is A (HF).

questions.question: A compound has molecules with non-polar bonds and permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces between its molecules. Which could be its formula, using the Data Booklet? A: NO; B: BeCl2; C: PH3; D: CI4.
steps: Non-polar bonds need almost equal electronegativity: P and H differ very little, so P-H bonds are essentially non-polar.
PH3 is pyramidal, so its bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule has a permanent dipole.
A (NO) has clearly polar bonds, so it does not fit the first condition.
B (BeCl2) has polar bonds but is linear and symmetrical, so the molecule has no permanent dipole.
D (CI4) is a symmetrical tetrahedron, so it has no permanent dipole.
So the answer is C (PH3).

questions.question: In which process are intermolecular hydrogen bonds broken? A: H2(g) -> 2H(g); B: H2O(l) -> H2O(g); C: H2(l) -> H2(g); D: H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> H2O(g).
steps: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular, so they are broken when molecules separate without breaking covalent bonds.
A breaks the covalent H-H bond within H2, not an intermolecular force.
C is changing state of H2, which breaks only London forces between H2 molecules.
D forms a covalent H-O bond, which is a chemical reaction and not an intermolecular change.
B: vaporising liquid water separates H2O molecules, breaking the hydrogen bonds between them.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: In which liquid solvent would the solubility of lithium chloride (LiCl) be lowest? A: ammonia; B: cyclohexane; C: methanol; D: water.
steps: LiCl is ionic and dissolves when its ions are attracted to polar solvent molecules (ion-dipole interactions).
Ammonia, methanol and water are polar and solvate the Li+ and Cl- ions.
Cyclohexane is non-polar, so it cannot form ion-dipole attractions to separate the ions.
So LiCl is least soluble in cyclohexane (B).

questions.question: Sodium chloride dissolves in water because of interactions between the sodium chloride and water. What are these interactions? A: dipole-dipole; B: hydrogen bonds; C: ion-dipole; D: London forces.
steps: NaCl is ionic, so it contains Na+ and Cl- ions rather than molecules.
Water is a polar molecule with partial charges on O and H.
Each ion is attracted to the oppositely charged end of water molecules, which is an ion-dipole interaction.
Dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonds and London forces do not describe attraction between ions and water molecules.
So the answer is C (ion-dipole).

questions.question: Which is the best solvent for chloroethane? A: ethanol; B: hexane; C: hydrochloric acid; D: water.
steps: Chloroethane (C2H5Cl) is a polar molecule with a permanent C-Cl dipole.
Like dissolves like: polar solutes dissolve best in polar solvents.
Ethanol is polar and has an alkyl chain, so it mixes with chloroethane through dipole-dipole and London forces.
Hexane is non-polar, so it cannot form strong attractions with the polar C-Cl bond.
Water and hydrochloric acid are aqueous and strongly hydrogen bonded, so they mix less well with chloroethane.
So the answer is A (ethanol).

questions.question: Draw a diagram to show hydrogen bonding between two H2O molecules in ice, including bond angles, relevant dipoles and lone pairs.
questions.answer: Two V-shaped H2O molecules with H-O-H angle about 104.5 deg, two lone pairs on each O, delta+ on H and delta- on O, and a dashed H-bond from the delta+ H of one molecule to a lone pair on the O of the other (angle close to 180 deg).
steps: Draw each water molecule as V-shaped with an H-O-H bond angle of about 104.5 deg.
Show two lone pairs on each O atom.
Label each O as delta- and each H as delta+, because the O-H bonds are polar.
Draw a dashed line from the delta+ H of one molecule to a lone pair on the O of the neighbouring molecule.
Label the O-H...O arrangement as close to linear (about 180 deg) and mark the charges on the hydrogen bond.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the effect of intermolecular forces on the properties of water and ammonia, using the data shown.
questions.answer: Both have hydrogen bonding, but water has far more per molecule, so it boils higher (373 K against 240 K), and ice is less dense than water
steps: Similar Mr (16.0 and 18.0), so differences come from intermolecular forces: both NH3 and H2O form hydrogen bonds (plus London forces).
Water has two delta+ H and two lone pairs on O, so each molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds; NH3 has three H but only one lone pair, so fewer.
More energy is needed to break water's hydrogen bonds, so water has the higher boiling temperature (373 K against 240 K).
At 223 K water is ice (926 kg m^-3), less dense than liquid water (1000 kg m^-3 at 278 K): hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice with large gaps.
NH3 at 278 K is a gas (0.763 kg m^-3) since it boils at 240 K, whereas water is still a dense liquid at 278 K because its hydrogen bonds hold the molecules together.

questions.question: Which is the best estimate for the boiling temperature of HBr? A: 59 deg C; B: -20 deg C; C: -67 deg C; D: -90 deg C.
steps: The boiling temperatures of hydrogen halides rise with molecular mass because London forces get stronger: HCl < HBr < HI.
HCl boils at about -85 deg C and HI at about -35 deg C, so HBr must lie between these values.
A (59 deg C) is far above HI, so it breaks the trend.
B (-20 deg C) is above HI (-35 deg C), so it breaks the trend.
D (-90 deg C) is below HCl (-85 deg C), so it breaks the trend.
So C (-67 deg C) is the best estimate.

questions.question: Why does HF not fit the pattern of boiling temperatures of the other hydrogen halides? A: it forms hydrogen bonds; B: it is much smaller than the other hydrogen halides; C: the other halogens are all electronegative; D: fluorine is the most reactive.
steps: The boiling temperatures of HCl, HBr and HI rise with molecular mass because of London forces.
HF boils much higher than this trend predicts.
In HF the H is bonded to very electronegative F, so hydrogen bonds form between molecules.
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than London forces, so more energy is needed to boil HF.
B, C and D do not explain the extra strength of the intermolecular forces.
So the answer is A.

questions.question: Which amine with molecular formula C3H9N has the lowest boiling temperature? A: (CH3)3N; B: CH3CH2NHCH3; C: CH3CH2CH2NH2; D: CH3CH(NH2)CH3.
steps: Amines with N-H bonds can form hydrogen bonds between molecules.
B, C and D are secondary or primary amines, each with at least one N-H bond.
A, (CH3)3N, is a tertiary amine with no N-H bond, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds.
Without hydrogen bonds, (CH3)3N has only dipole-dipole and London forces, which are weaker.
So A has the lowest boiling temperature.
